title: Center of Polygon Finder: Centroid on the Map
description: Find a representative centre for any drawn area with the Center of Polygon Finder — the centroid for labels, origins and distance work. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, an L-shaped parcel made of a 200×100 ft block and a 100×100 ft block has its centroid at the area-weighted point (83.3, 83.3) in local feet — not at the middle of its bounding box.
quick_answer: The Center of Polygon Finder computes a centre — the centroid — for an area you draw on the map. It balances the shape's area the way a balance point balances weight, giving you a point to label, measure distances from, or hand to another tool as the area's origin.

Reducing polygons to representative points is a daily GIS operation. This is that operation without the software stack — same area-weighted principle.

Block A: 200×100 ft (20,000 sq ft, centre 100, 50). Block B: 100×100 ft on top of A's left half (10,000 sq ft, centre 50, 150). The combined centroid is the area-weighted average: ((20,000×100 + 10,000×50) ÷ 30,000, same for y) = (83.3, 83.3) ft — pulled toward the bigger block, as it should be.
For a regular shape the centroid is the obvious middle: a square field's centre is its centre. The tool earns its keep on the shapes where 'obvious' fails — crescents, L's and donuts.

popular_table.note: For label placement on awkward shapes, the pole of inaccessibility (centre of the largest inscribed circle) beats the centroid; for distance origins and balance, the centroid is the standard.

faq: It is the area centroid of the polygon you draw, computed with the standard shoelace-weighted formula on the map's geometry. For typical parcel shapes it matches a GIS centroid to well within drawing accuracy.
Why is my centre outside the shape?

Crescent, C and donut shapes have centroids in their holes or bays — mathematically correct, occasionally awkward. For a label point that must sit inside, choose a point near the centroid that lies within the boundary.
Centroid or centre of the bounding box?
They differ exactly when the shape is irregular. The bounding-box centre ignores where the area is; the centroid weights it. For L-shaped land the difference is tens of metres.
Can I use the centre as a distance origin?
Yes — that is a primary use. Distances from a centroid are 'from the middle of the area' in the only defensible sense the phrase has.
Does it work for shapes drawn anywhere?
Yes — fields, territories, lakes (as outlines), districts. If it can be drawn as a polygon, it has a centroid.
What about a shape with a hole?
Draw the outer boundary for the gross centroid. For the net figure, most users draw the main mass; hole-aware centroiding is a GIS refinement.
Is a radius the same as driving distance?
Unrelated — this tool finds a point, not a distance. From that point, road questions belong to the routing tools.
